cf.title: plpgsql: detoast a returned record before keeping it in a non-atomic context

input.subject: [PATCH] plpgsql: detoast a returned record before keeping it in a non-atomic context

verdict_reasoning: No objection survived at levels 1a, 1b or 2. Message #1 states a reproducible failure on 14 through master and a fix that applies the detoast rule of 2efc924180f to one more assignment path. Confidence is low because only one message is visible and the code was not read.

brief.title: Detoast a PL/pgSQL function's returned record in a non-atomic context
brief.problem: In a DO block or procedure that can COMMIT or ROLLBACK, r := f() keeps the TOAST pointers of the record returned by a PL/pgSQL function. After a ROLLBACK, or after a COMMIT once the row is deleted and vacuumed, reading r fails with "missing chunk number 0 for toast value". CALL p(f()) fails the same way after the procedure's own ROLLBACK.
brief.proposed_design: exec_move_row_from_datum() still takes over a read/write expanded record of the right type, but in a non-atomic context it first inlines the record's out-of-line fields in place. It does this when ER_FLAG_HAVE_EXTERNAL is set, by computing the flat size, which detoasts each external field and clears the flag. Atomic contexts and records with no out-of-line fields are unchanged.
author_claims: The failure reproduces on master and on 14 through 19, in DO blocks and procedures.
The fix closes an oversight in 2efc924180f, which detoasts other assignment paths in a non-atomic context.
A loop of 100,000 such assignments leaves the backend's memory contexts unchanged, and inlining in place is cheaper than copying the record.
check-world (without TAP) passes on master, and PL/pgSQL tests pass under Valgrind; the patch cherry-picks cleanly to 14 through 19.
It should be back-patched to 14, as the similar fix f21fadafaf0 was back-patched to 11.
brief.thread_state: Only the first message is visible. The CommitFest entry is in Needs review, with no reviewer named.
unclear: The material gives no timing for the extra detoast cost when a non-atomic block assigns large records many times.
The patch does not say whether other paths that take over expanded objects, such as expanded arrays or OUT parameters, have the same gap.
The material does not say whether the new step covers the CALL p(f()) case or only the DO block assignment.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: The author asks for a back-patch to 14 through 19 and tags the entry Backport.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The patch adds one more detoast step in pl_exec.c that future takeover paths must also follow.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: Non-atomic r := f() now detoasts each out-of-line field of the returned record on assignment.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: Does the new step in exec_move_row_from_datum() also fix CALL p(f()), and does a test cover that case?
Do other paths that take over an expanded object in a non-atomic context, such as expanded arrays or OUT parameters, have the same gap?
What is the time cost when a non-atomic block assigns a record with large out-of-line fields many times, compared with unpatched master?
Do the TAP tests pass on master and on each back branch with the patch?

committability.owner_note: A committer who knows PL/pgSQL's expanded-record handling and the non-atomic detoast rules of 2efc924180f would have to own it. None has spoken in the visible thread.
committability.liability: The owner signs for a behaviour change in six branches, 14 through master: correctness of in-place detoast of a taken-over record, and any memory or timing change in minor releases.
committability.author_follow_up: No sign either way; only message #1 is visible. The author tested each back branch and ran Valgrind, which suggests care.

priority.reason: The patch is about 5 KiB, touches pl_exec.c and one isolation test, and fixes a reproducible "missing chunk number 0" error in non-atomic blocks. The entry has no reviewer, and a back-patch needs a committer who knows PL/pgSQL.

provisional_note: Without the code, nobody checked that ER_get_flat_size() inlines fields in the right memory context and leaves the record valid for takeover. Whether the CALL p(f()) path reaches the new step is also unchecked.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Rearrange execution of PARAM_EXTERN Params for plpgsql's benefit.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Rearrange execution of PARAM_EXTERN Params for plpgsql's benefit.
Reverted commit(s): Further reduce overhead for passing plpgsql variables to the executor.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This patch does three interrelated things:

* Create a new expression execution step type EEOP_PARAM_CALLBACK
and add the infrastructure needed for add-on modules to generate that.
As discussed, the best control mechanism for that seems to be to add
another hook function to ParamListInfo, which will be called by
ExecInitExpr if it's supplied and a PARAM_EXTERN Param is found.
For stand-alone expressions, we add a new entry point to allow the
ParamListInfo to be specified directly, since it can't be retrieved
from the parent plan node's EState.

* Redesign the API for the ParamListInfo paramFetch hook so that the
ParamExternData array can be entirely virtual.  This also lets us get rid
of ParamListInfo.paramMask, instead leaving it to the paramFetch hook to
decide which param IDs should be accessible or not.  plpgsql_param_fetch
was already doing the identical masking check, so having callers do it too
seemed redundant.  While I was at it, I added a "speculative" flag to
paramFetch that the planner can specify as TRUE to avoid unwanted failures.
This solves an ancient problem for plpgsql that it couldn't provide values
of non-DTYPE_VAR variables to the planner for fear of triggering premature
"record not assigned yet" or "field not found" errors during planning.

* Rework plpgsql to get rid of the need for "unshared" parameter lists,
by dint of turning the single ParamListInfo per estate into a nearly
read-only data structure that doesn't instantiate any per-variable data.
Instead, the paramFetch hook controls access to per-variable data and can
make the right decisions on the fly, replacing the cases that we used to
need multiple ParamListInfos for.  This might perhaps have been a
performance loss on its own, but by using a paramCompile hook we can
bypass plpgsql_param_fetch entirely during normal query execution.
(It's now only called when, eg, we copy the ParamListInfo into a cursor
portal.  copyParamList() or SerializeParamList() effectively instantiate
the virtual parameter array as a simple physical array without a
paramFetch hook, which is what we want in those cases.)  This allows
reverting most of commit 6c82d8d1f, though I kept the cosmetic
code-consolidation aspects of that (eg the assign_simple_var function).

Performance testing shows this to be at worst a break-even change,
and it can provide wins ranging up to 20% in test cases involving
accesses to fields of "record" variables.  The fact that values of
such variables can now be exposed to the planner might produce wins
in some situations, too, but I've not pursued that angle.

In passing, remove the "parent" pointer from the arguments to
ExecInitExprRec and related functions, instead storing that pointer in a
transient field in ExprState.  The ParamListInfo pointer for a stand-alone
expression is handled the same way; we'd otherwise have had to add
yet another recursively-passed-down argument in expression compilation.

precedents_retrieved.title: iteration over record in plpgsql
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a row_to_array function that turns any row into a text array of field names and values. It also extends plpgsql FOREACH so a list of target variables, such as key and value, can take consecutive elements of an array in one step.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that row_to_array casts all fields to text and drops SQL datatypes, and said row_to_json already covers the case. He also asked that the two features be split and that FOREACH get its own discussion. Jim Nasby worried that the FOREACH pairing rule would block iteration that follows array dimensions. The later messages move to typed iteration over records and broader dynamic typing, and no revised design was agreed.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
While I don't have a problem with hstore_to_array, I don't think that
row_to_array is a very good idea; it's basically encouraging people to
throw away SQL datatypes altogether and imagine that everything is text.

precedents_retrieved.title: Expand applicability of aggregate's sortop optimization
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets the planner keep the index-based MIN/MAX optimization for aggregates with an ORDER BY clause, such as MIN(x ORDER BY x), when the ordering uses the same column and a sort operator from the same btree opfamily as the aggregate's sortop. Later in the thread, Andrei Lepikhov reworked it into an aggregate support function (prosupport) that removes the aggregate's ORDER BY for min/max.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane reviewed the prosupport version and found no documentation for the new support request. He doubted that sharing a btree opfamily justifies removing the ORDER BY clause, given opposite sort directions and plans without an index. He also found no check that the aggregated and ordering expressions match, and questioned whether MIN(x ORDER BY x) occurs often enough to be worth the planning cycles. The original author then closed the entry because the patch had become a different patch, and suggested a new entry for it.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Also, I am far from convinced that the code is right: the fact that the aggsortop shares a btree opfamily with orderClause->sortop doesn't seem to be enough to justify removing the aggorder clause.

precedents_retrieved.title: Return ERROR on COMMIT instead of silently ROLLBACK
precedents_retrieved.summary: Make COMMIT of an aborted transaction raise an error instead of silently returning the ROLLBACK command tag, as the SQL standard requires. The transaction still ends, and the patch added a new USER_ERROR message level so that COMMIT could report the error.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Review found that the USER_ERROR level is a kluge: libpq still saw PGRES_COMMAND_OK for the failed COMMIT, and COMMIT AND CHAIN still started a new transaction after the error. No one agreed on what COMMIT AND CHAIN should do in this case. The patch also failed on the cfbot, and the author said the approach was too simple and that he did not plan to rewrite it.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: So I think we should not introduce USER_ERROR at all.

precedents_retrieved.title: Statement-level rollback
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds `START TRANSACTION ROLLBACK SCOPE { TRANSACTION | STATEMENT }` and a `default_transaction_rollback_scope` GUC, so a failed statement rolls back only itself and the transaction continues. The server creates a savepoint before each top-level statement, and before each extended-protocol message, then releases it afterwards.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch stayed in Waiting on Author for the whole commitfest with no rebased version, so it was returned with feedback; Simon Riggs had offered to review an updated patch. Earlier, Tom Lane objected that the change would run into the compatibility problems that ended server-side autocommit, and suggested a client-side facility. The visible messages do not resolve that objection.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Since this patch was Waiting for author during the entire commitfest without updates, I’m marking it Returned with Feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Expand the use of check_canonical_path() for more GUCs
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch applied check_canonical_path() to more path GUCs: promote_trigger_file, krb_server_keyfile and the ssl_* file settings. It also added comments in guc.c explaining why data_directory, config_file, hba_file and ident_file already get canonicalized at postmaster startup.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Peter Eisentraut questioned why any GUC needs check_canonical_path(); he found the remaining calls in guc.c were leftovers from when data_directory and config_file were canonicalized there, and noted that canonicalize_path() does not make relative paths absolute. Tom Lane said user-given strings should not be altered without need, and that canonicalization matters only where other paths are derived from the value. The author concluded there was consensus to perhaps remove some canonicalization but not to expand it.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Yes, that's fair as there is visibly a consensus that we could perhaps
remove some of the canonicalization, but not expand it.

precedents_retrieved.title: Statement-level rollback
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a transaction rollback scope (START TRANSACTION ROLLBACK SCOPE { TRANSACTION | STATEMENT } and a default_transaction_rollback_scope GUC) so a failed statement rolls back only itself, not the whole transaction. The server creates a savepoint before each statement and releases it after, including for each extended query protocol message.
precedents_retrieved.objection: No new patch version was posted after Thomas Munro's November 2017 review, so the entry was returned with feedback in the last CF. Andres Freund also noted that there was no agreement on the design. Tom Lane had objected at the start that server-side behavior would hit the same compatibility problems that ended server-side autocommit, and he suggested a client-side facility instead.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Given that no new version has been submitted since, that this is the
last CF, and that we are far from agreeing on a design, I'm marking this
as returned with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Dynamic result sets from procedures
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets a procedure return multiple result sets to the client by declaring cursors with `DECLARE ... CURSOR WITH RETURN` in its body, following DB2 and the SQL standard. A companion psql patch prints every result set of a command, where psql now shows only the last one.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Daniel Verite found bugs in the psql part: `\gexec` drops the first result and fails with FETCH_COUNT, multiple result sets do not work with FETCH_COUNT, `\errverbose` loses the last error, and PGresults leak. The author did not answer for two weeks, so Michael Paquier returned the patch with feedback. Robert Haas also asked whether one command returning several results breaks applications, and the author replied that the wire protocol already supports it.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Peter, are you planning to answer to those complains? For now I am switching the patch as returned with feedback as this thread has no activity for two weeks.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Change default value of default_toast_compression to "lz4""
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Change default value of default_toast_compression to "lz4""
Reverted commit(s): Change default value of default_toast_compression to "lz4", when available
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit 7c1849311e49, due to the fact that more than 60% of
the buildfarm members do not have lz4 installed.  As we are in the last
commit fest of the development cycle, and that it could take a couple
of weeks to stabilize things, this change is reverted for now.

This commit will be reworked in a lighter version, as
default_toast_compression's default can be changed to "lz4" without the
switch from --with-lz4 to --without-lz4.  This approach will keep the
buildfarm at bay, and still allow builds to take advantage of LZ4 in
TOAST by default, as long as the code is compiled with LZ4 support.

A harder requirement based on LZ4 should be achievable at some point,
but it is going to require some work from the buildfarm owners first.
Perhaps this part could be revisited at the beginning of the next
development cycle.

precedents_retrieved.title: When deleting the plpgsql function, release the CachedPlan of the function
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Matthias van de Meent, Tom Lane
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch frees the CachedPlan contexts of a PL/pgSQL function or procedure when DROP FUNCTION or DROP PROCEDURE runs, so they no longer stay in CacheMemoryContext until the session ends. The author showed with pg_get_backend_memory_contexts() that a dropped and recreated procedure leaves two sets of CachedPlan contexts.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch frees cached plans only in the backend that runs the DROP, because other sessions do not execute RemoveFunctionById and keep their plans. Tom Lane suggested that PL/pgSQL, or funccache.c so SQL functions also benefit, install a shared-cache-invalidation callback on pg_proc that marks function trees as deletable. The author agreed, linked a new thread, and withdrew this entry. Vladlen Popolitov also asked why the plans should be freed at all.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: It doesn't, which is (one reason) why it's just a crude hack.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert applying column aliases to the output of whole-row Vars.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert applying column aliases to the output of whole-row Vars.
Reverted commit(s): Ensure that RowExprs and whole-row Vars produce the expected column names.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
In commit bf7ca1587, I had the bright idea that we could make the
result of a whole-row Var (that is, foo.*) track any column aliases
that had been applied to the FROM entry the Var refers to.  However,
that's not terribly logically consistent, because now the output of
the Var is no longer of the named composite type that the Var claims
to emit.  bf7ca1587 tried to handle that by changing the output
tuple values to be labeled with a blessed RECORD type, but that's
really pretty disastrous: we can wind up storing such tuples onto
disk, whereupon they're not readable by other sessions.

The only practical fix I can see is to give up on what bf7ca1587
tried to do, and say that the column names of tuples produced by
a whole-row Var are always those of the underlying named composite
type, query aliases or no.  While this introduces some inconsistencies,
it removes others, so it's not that awful in the abstract.  What *is*
kind of awful is to make such a behavioral change in a back-patched
bug fix.  But corrupt data is worse, so back-patched it will be.

(A workaround available to anyone who's unhappy about this is to
introduce an extra level of sub-SELECT, so that the whole-row Var is
referring to the sub-SELECT's output and not to a named table type.
Then the Var is of type RECORD to begin with and there's no issue.)

Per report from Miles Delahunty.  The faulty commit dates to 9.5,
so back-patch to all supported branches.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent found in the provided list, and the thread names no rejected attempt at this idea. Message #1 cites earlier fixes in the same area (2efc924180f, f21fadafaf0) and bug #17669 as related accepted work. The patch presents itself as closing an oversight in that work, so no earlier rejection reason applies.

From the standards and compatibility angle there is nothing to object to. The patch adds no syntax, keyword, GUC, catalog object, dump content or psql change. The only behaviour change is that r := f() and CALL p(f()) in a non-atomic context no longer fail with "missing chunk number 0", which is the same detoast-on-assignment rule that 2efc924180f already applies to every other assignment path. Existing scripts that work today keep working after a minor upgrade, so the back-patch does not alter a user-facing contract. I could not check, without the code, whether the extra detoast changes memory or timing for large records. That belongs to the performance angle.

The patch touches only in-memory PL/pgSQL handling in pl_exec.c, plus an isolation test. It changes no on-disk format, WAL record, catalog, wire protocol or exported struct, so pg_upgrade, standbys and back-patch ABI are unaffected.

The patch only changes when Postgres detoasts a record that a PL/pgSQL function has already returned to the caller, so no one can read data they could not read before. It adds no privilege, role, GUC or SQL surface. The extra memory use matches what the other non-atomic assignment paths have done since 2efc924180f.

From the maintenance and fit angle there is nothing to reject. The patch is a small fix in pl_exec.c that follows the rule commit 2efc924180f already set for other assignment paths. Its cost applies only to non-atomic blocks that assign a record with out-of-line fields, and those blocks already pay the same detoast cost on every other assignment path. It adds no API, GUC, catalog or format change, so a back-patch commits the project to nothing new. Two points cannot be checked from the material: whether CALL p(f()) goes through the same code path, and whether other takeover paths have the same gap. A committer who knows PL/pgSQL should confirm both before back-patching. No such committer has engaged in the visible thread yet.

This is a bug fix that brings exec_move_row_from_datum() into line with the existing detoast rule for non-atomic contexts. Postgres has no existing feature, extension or hook that gives the same guarantee. Users can copy the field into a local variable, but that is a workaround for a crash, so no already-exists objection applies.

This is a bug fix, so demand is not in question. Message #1 shows a reproducible read failure ("missing chunk number 0") on 14 through master, reached through ordinary DO blocks and procedures, and links it to bug #17669, where a non-atomic procedure was the suggested workaround and now fails the same way. The cost falls only on non-atomic assignments of records that hold out-of-line fields.
